name: THE EGGPLANT ONE ON ME BURGER

recipe.history:
Eggplant — known as aubergine in much of the world and as 'nasu' in Japan — has a culinary history stretching back over four thousand years to the Indian subcontinent, where it was first domesticated and integrated into the cooking of South Asia. From India, eggplant traveled along trade routes into Persia, the Arab world, and eventually the Mediterranean, arriving in Europe by the 12th century through Moorish Spain and North Africa. Each culture it encountered adapted it according to its own culinary logic: the Italians battered and fried it into eggplant parmigiana, the Greeks layered it into moussaka, the Levantine world transformed it into baba ghanoush, and the Japanese mastered it in the form of nasu dengaku — grilled eggplant lacquered with a sweet white miso glaze and broiled until the flesh becomes creamy and the glaze caramelizes into something close to toffee. It is this Japanese preparation that defines this burger, and it represents one of the most sophisticated uses of a vegetable in the global grilling tradition.

Eggplant came to the American burger world through the vegetarian and plant-forward burger movement of the 2000s and 2010s, but the more interesting story is how miso-glazed eggplant crossed over into meat-centric cooking, landing on burgers not as a substitute for beef but as a companion to it. The umami of white miso is among the deepest savory flavors in any culinary tradition, and when it caramelizes on grilled eggplant it produces a complexity that amplifies rather than competes with beef fat. Restaurant chefs began adding planks of miso-glazed eggplant to wagyu and dry-aged beef burgers in the 2010s, discovering that the soft, smoky, caramelized vegetable added a textural and flavor dimension that no cheese or sauce alone could provide. The eggplant became a revelation: proof that a vegetable could make a beef burger more beefy.

I grew up thinking I hated eggplant. Every version I encountered as a child was either waterlogged and bitter or rubbery and bland, and I carried that prejudice for years until a friend made me a bowl of nasu dengaku at a dinner party in my late twenties. The eggplant had been halved, scored in a crosshatch, brushed with white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar, and broiled until the surface was almost black in places and the flesh beneath had collapsed into a silky, sweet, savory cream. I ate three pieces standing at the counter before dinner was served and have never looked at eggplant the same way again. I put it on a burger within the week.

Medium rare beef — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius — is the necessary foundation for this burger because the richness of the miso-glazed eggplant requires a counterpart of equal substance. Eggplant at its best is luxurious: soft, oily, deeply savory, with a sweetness from the caramelized miso. Placed on overcooked beef, all of that luxury is wasted — the eggplant's richness amplifies the dryness and chewiness of a well-done patty and the whole thing becomes muddy and heavy. On a medium rare patty, the eggplant finds its complement: the juicy, pink, mineral-forward beef and the caramelized, earthy eggplant exist in balance, each making the other taste more fully like itself. Cook to medium rare. Everything else follows.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.

2. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle sesame seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.
3. Make the miso glaze: Whisk together white miso, mirin, sake, sugar, soy sauce, and sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth.

4. Prepare the eggplant: Score the cut side of each eggplant half in a crosshatch pattern about 1/2 inch deep, being careful not to cut through the skin. Brush lightly with neutral oil on the cut side. Heat a grill pan or cast iron skillet over medium-high heat. Place eggplant cut-side down and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the flesh is golden and softened.

5. Flip eggplant halves skin-side down. Brush the cut side generously with miso glaze. Transfer to a baking sheet. Broil on high for 3 to 5 minutes until the glaze is caramelized, bubbling, and deeply browned in spots. Watch closely to prevent burning. Remove and set aside.
6. Make the sesame aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, tahini, sesame oil, rice vinegar, soy sauce, and garlic. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Shape patties: Season ground beef with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 equal portions and shape into patties 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple into the center of each.
8. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties undisturbed 3 minutes.
9. Flip and cook 2 to 3 more minutes, monitoring temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Remove at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
10. Toast buns cut-side down in residual skillet fat for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

11. Assemble: Spread sesame aioli on both cut sides of the bun. Place a leaf of butter lettuce on the bottom bun, then the patty. Lay one miso-glazed eggplant half (or both halves from one eggplant, depending on size) over the patty. Scatter sliced scallions and sesame seeds over the top. Close the bun and serve immediately.
